title: Judicial Activism and PIL

cards.h: When courts act for the people
cards.b:
India's Supreme Court is among the most powerful in the world. Public Interest Litigation (PIL) and judicial activism opened justice to the poor but also raised the charge of judicial overreach. This is a standard Paper I theme and appears in essays.

The idea began with Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer in the late 1970s. Hussainara Khatoon (1979), on undertrial prisoners, is an early landmark case.

Judicial activism is a proactive role in protecting rights and filling gaps; restraint is deference to the legislature. The term is credited to Arthur Schlesinger (1947).

In India, after the Emergency, the Court sought to repair its image (ADM Jabalpur, 1976). Judges P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer relaxed locus standi and let letters count as petitions (epistolary jurisdiction). Basis: Art. 32 (Supreme Court) and Art. 226 (High Courts).
Hussainara Khatoon was the first big PIL, on speedy trial under Art. 21.

In Maneka Gandhi (1978) the Court said that 'procedure established by law' must be fair, just and reasonable. From that, it read into Art. 21 the rights to livelihood (Olga Tellis, 1985), clean environment, education (Unni Krishnan, 1993), privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), dignity, health and food. Other PIL directions: D.K. Basu (1997) arrest guidelines; Vineet Narain (1997) on CBI independence; Prakash Singh (2006) police reform; NALSA (2014) recognised transgender persons.

The Court even took charge of its own appointments. Second Judges Case (1993) and the Third Judges Case advisory (1998) created the collegium. In 2015 it struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC as violating the basic structure (independence of the judiciary). Critics find the collegium opaque and self-perpetuating.

Any bona fide person or group can approach the Supreme Court or a High Court for the benefit of those who cannot, such as the poor, prisoners or bonded workers. The Court may treat a letter as a writ petition, appoint commissions to find facts, name an amicus curiae to assist, and issue continuing mandamus to monitor compliance. The usual rules of standing, pleadings and court fees are relaxed. In 2010 (Balwant Singh Chaufal) the Court laid down guidelines to screen out private or frivolous petitions.

• Separation of powers: courts making policy, such as the Delhi CNG order and the 2012 2G licence cancellation.
  • Misuse of PIL: 'publicity interest litigation', frivolous cases. The Court has imposed costs and set 2010 guidelines.
  • No accountability or expertise on technical matters.
  • Defenders: executive failure forces courts to act, as in Vishaka, where Parliament was silent until 2013.

The Court now says PIL must be bona fide, with real public interest and not personal or political gain. Courts increasingly issue continuing mandamus and monitor implementation. Judgments recently stress constitutional morality (Navtej Johar, 2018; Joseph Shine, 2018, adultery), and the earlier 'positive' rights reading for socio-economic rights (Part IV).

Examples to cite: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, basic structure), Puttaswamy (2017 privacy), Right to food (PUCL), environment (Forest cases, Vellore Citizens, 1996, 'polluter pays'), electoral bonds struck down (15 February 2024). Also relevant: the 'Judicial vs executive' friction over appointments, with Law Ministry and the Collegium.

"Judicial activism is a necessary supplement to democracy but not a substitute. Discuss."
"Examine the role of PIL in expanding access to justice in India."
"Distinguish judicial activism from judicial overreach with examples."

Structure: definition, origins, landmark cases, Art. 21, appointments, critique, safeguards, examples.

Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) is a classic example: the Court laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace until Parliament acted.
